Percentage Points vs Percent Change in Grades

Learn the difference between percentage-point gains and relative percent increases, with grade, exam-weight and target examples.

By GradeTargetCalc · Published 2 November 2026 · 5 min read

In this guide
Two descriptions can refer to the same improvementCalculate the percentage-point difference firstUse the original value for a relative percent increaseTranslate an assessment change into course percentage pointsRead “increase by ten percent” carefullyAn increase and its reversal need different relative percentagesChoose wording that makes the basis visibleFAQsSources
01

Two descriptions can refer to the same improvement

A mark rises from 64% to 72%. Someone calls it an eight-point improvement; another person says it increased by 12.5%. Those statements can both be correct, but they measure different things. Percentage points describe the direct distance between two percentage values. Percent change compares that distance with the starting value.

In academic planning, the distinction matters when discussing reassessments, estimating a weighted course gain or setting a target. Using “eight percent” without naming the basis can lead someone to calculate a different result from the one you intended.

02

Calculate the percentage-point difference first

Percentage-point change = New percentage − Original percentage. Moving from 64% to 72% gives 72 − 64 = eight percentage points. The subtraction uses the same percentage scale on both sides. Moving from 88% to 96% also gains eight percentage points.

For a decrease, retain the sign when it helps interpretation. A fall from 72% to 64% is a change of minus eight percentage points, or an eight-percentage-point decrease. This direct distance is usually the clearest wording for a course grade because the grade itself is already expressed as a percentage.

03

Use the original value for a relative percent increase

Relative percent change = (New − Original) ÷ Original × 100. For 64% rising to 72%, divide the eight-point difference by 64 and multiply by 100. The relative increase is 12.5%. Starting at 88% and gaining eight points instead produces approximately 9.09%.

The same absolute gain therefore has a larger relative size when the starting score is lower. If the starting value is zero, this standard relative-change formula is undefined because it divides by zero. A rise from zero to 20% can be described as twenty percentage points without assigning a finite relative percentage increase.

04

Translate an assessment change into course percentage points

Suppose a project worth 25% of a course is replaced from 64% to 72%, with all other contributions unchanged. The assessment improves by eight percentage points, but its effect on the course is 8 × 0.25 = two course percentage points. A current overall grade of 70% would become 72% under that replacement model.

The project’s 12.5% relative increase is not the multiplier to apply to the whole course. Multiplying 70 by 1.125 would incorrectly give 78.75%. That calculation assumes the entire course result improves proportionally, rather than changing one quarter-weight assessment by a known amount.

05

Read “increase by ten percent” carefully

Starting from 70%, a ten-percentage-point increase reaches 80%. A ten-percent relative increase reaches 70 × 1.10 = 77%. If your planning conversation uses the shorter phrase “improve by ten percent,” ask whether it refers to ten points on the grade scale or ten percent of the existing score.

A target grade of 80% does not require converting the gap into a relative increase before using a grade calculator. Enter the target directly in the tool designed for that question. Relative change is useful for describing a comparison; it is usually unnecessary for solving a weighted academic target.

06

An increase and its reversal need different relative percentages

Going from 64% to 72% is a 12.5% relative increase. Returning from 72% to 64% is an 8 ÷ 72 × 100 = 11.11…% relative decrease. The percentage-point change has the same magnitude in both directions, while the relative percentage changes because its starting denominator changes.

This is also why two successive ten-percent relative increases do not equal twenty percentage points. Starting at 50%, the first reaches 55% and the second reaches 60.5%. Each increase uses a new base. Avoid applying compound-growth language to grading rules unless the rule genuinely operates that way.

07

Choose wording that makes the basis visible

When sharing a result, include the before-and-after scores and the unit. “My project increased from 64% to 72%, adding two points to a course where it counts 25%” communicates more than an isolated claim that your grade improved by a percentage.

If you are comparing practice tests, record their question totals and marking rules too. A change in percentages does not establish equal assessment difficulty or equal learning gains. The arithmetic describes the observed scores; interpreting progress still requires comparable tasks and useful feedback.

  • Subtract percentages to report an absolute percentage-point change.
  • Divide that change by the original value only when relative change is the question.
  • Apply assessment weight to the absolute score change when estimating its course impact.
  • Label rounded comparisons as approximate when the underlying fraction continues.
Quick answers

Frequently asked questions

Is a 5% increase always five percentage points?

No. A relative five-percent increase multiplies the original value by 1.05. Five percentage points are added directly to a percentage grade. State which meaning applies.

Can a percentage-point change be negative?

Yes. A new mark below the original produces a negative difference. You can report that sign or describe the magnitude as a percentage-point decrease.

Which number belongs in the grade-improvement calculator?

Enter the actual old and new assessment percentages and its course weight. The tool computes the course-point effect without requiring a relative percent-change input.
